prompt: A storefront lighting load is 16 A and will run more than 3 hours. Terminations are 75°C. What is the smallest copper THHN branch-circuit size and OCPD that meet the 210.19/210.20 continuous-load factors?

options.text: 12 AWG copper on a 20 A breaker
14 AWG copper on a 15 A breaker
12 AWG copper on a 15 A breaker
10 AWG copper on a 25 A breaker

explanation: A continuous load is one expected to run 3 hours or more. Branch-circuit conductors and the OCPD must be sized at not less than 125% of that load: 16 A × 1.25 = 20 A. 12 AWG copper is the smallest size 240.4(D) permits on a 20 A breaker, and its 75°C ampacity (25 A) covers 20 A.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the 16 A nameplate without the 125% continuous factor and violates the 240.4(D) 15 A cap only as if the load were noncontinuous 14 AWG work.
distractorExplanations.c: The 12 AWG conductor can carry 20 A, but 210.20 still requires the OCPD itself to be at least 125% of the continuous load (20 A), not 15 A.
distractorExplanations.d: Oversizes both the conductor and breaker; 25 A is not required once 16 A × 1.25 is 20 A, and it wastes material on this branch.

prompt: A 60 A copper feeder supplies a subpanel. What equipment grounding conductor size does Table 250.122 require, independent of the ungrounded conductor size?

options.text: 8 AWG copper, the 100 A row of Table 250.122
10 AWG copper, the 60 A overcurrent-device row
6 AWG copper, matching typical 60 A ungrounded conductors
Size the EGC from Table 250.66 using the ungrounded conductors

explanation: Equipment grounding conductors are sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit, not by matching the ungrounded conductors and not from Table 250.66. For a 60 A OCPD the copper EGC is 10 AWG. Upsize the EGC only if you increase ungrounded conductors for voltage drop (250.122(B)).

distractorExplanations.a: Reads the 100 A row of Table 250.122 (8 AWG copper). A 60 A feeder uses the 60 A row, which is 10 AWG copper.
distractorExplanations.c: Matches the EGC to typical 6 AWG ungrounded conductors. Table 250.122 follows the OCPD rating, so 60 A still takes 10 AWG copper.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the EGC with the grounding electrode conductor. Table 250.66 sizes the GEC from ungrounded service conductors, not feeder EGCs.

prompt: Four 10 AWG copper THHN current-carrying conductors share one EMT at 30°C. Terminations are 75°C. What ampacity do you use when selecting the branch OCPD?

options.text: 40 A, 90°C column with no adjustment
35 A, 75°C column with no CCC adjustment
32 A, 90°C value times 80% for four CCC
30 A, applying the 70% factor for four CCC

explanation: THHN may start at the 90°C column of Table 310.16 (10 AWG copper = 40 A) for adjustment, but 310.15(C)(1) requires 80% when four to six current-carrying conductors share a raceway: 40 A × 0.80 = 32 A. That 32 A is below the 75°C termination value (35 A), so 32 A governs OCPD selection.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the 90°C column as a termination rating. 110.14(C) limits terminations to 75°C unless the equipment is 90°C-listed, and four CCC still require the 80% adjustment.
distractorExplanations.b: Takes the 75°C column (35 A) without the 80% adjustment required for four current-carrying conductors in one raceway.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the 70% factor, which is the 7–9 CCC row of 310.15(C)(1), not the 4–6 conductor 80% row.

prompt: A metal device box contains four 12 AWG insulated conductors, one 12 AWG equipment grounding conductor, one internal cable clamp, and one wiring device. What minimum box volume does 314.16 require?

options.text: 13.50 in³, counting the yoke as one 12 AWG volume
15.75 in³, omitting the equipment grounding conductor
11.25 in³, counting only the four insulated conductors
18.00 in³, using 2.25 in³ for each 12 AWG allowance

explanation: Table 314.16(B) assigns 2.25 in³ per 12 AWG volume. Four insulated conductors = 9.00; all EGCs together count as one volume = 2.25; one or more internal clamps = 2.25; each yoke counts as two volumes = 4.50. Total 18.00 in³. Fill is a volume check, not an ampacity or conduit-fill check.

distractorExplanations.a: Counts the device yoke as a single 12 AWG volume (2.25). 314.16(B)(4) requires two volume allowances for each yoke.
distractorExplanations.b: Drops the EGC allowance. One or more EGCs still add one volume based on the largest EGC in the box (here 2.25 in³).
distractorExplanations.c: Counts only the four insulated conductors (9.00) plus one extra 2.25, ignoring clamp, EGC, and the double yoke allowance.

prompt: A 200 A, 120/240 V service uses 3/0 copper ungrounded conductors. The grounding electrode conductor lands only on a single driven rod. What is the smallest copper GEC Table 250.66 with 250.66(A) permits?

options.text: 6 AWG copper, the rod-electrode ceiling in 250.66(A)
4 AWG copper, the full Table 250.66 size for 3/0 copper
8 AWG copper, the smallest GEC in Table 250.66
2 AWG copper, the row used for 250 kcmil ungrounded conductors

explanation: Table 250.66 would size a GEC for 3/0 copper ungrounded conductors at 4 AWG copper. When that GEC connects solely to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode, 250.66(A) does not require it larger than 6 AWG copper. 8 AWG is the table minimum for small services, not a further reduction off a 3/0 service.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the full Table 250.66 size for 3/0 (4 AWG) and skips 250.66(A), which caps a rod-only GEC at 6 AWG copper.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops to 8 AWG, the Table 250.66 size for 2 AWG or smaller ungrounded conductors. 250.66(A) reduces 4 AWG to 6 AWG, not to 8 AWG.
distractorExplanations.d: Reads a larger Table 250.66 row (2 AWG for 3/0 aluminum through 250 kcmil copper). 3/0 copper is the 4 AWG copper row before the rod cap.

prompt: A 480Y/277 V switchboard has exposed live parts on both sides of the working space (Table 110.26(A)(1) Condition 3). What is the minimum clear working depth?

options.text: 3 ft, the 0–150 V Condition 1 depth
4 ft, the 151–600 V Condition 3 depth
3½ ft, the 151–600 V Condition 2 depth
6 ft, the dedicated equipment-space height in 110.26(E)

explanation: Voltage to ground on a 480Y/277 V system is 277 V, so the 151–600 V column applies. Condition 3 is exposed live parts on both sides of the working space, which requires 4 ft of clear depth. Width and height are separate 110.26(A)(2) and (A)(3) rules; 110.26(E) dedicated space is not working-depth.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the 0–150 V column and Condition 1. 277 V to ground is the 151–600 V column, and live-to-live is Condition 3.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses Condition 2 (live parts on one side, grounded on the other) at 151–600 V, which is 3½ ft, not live-to-live Condition 3.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses working-space depth with dedicated equipment space, which extends 6 ft above the gear or to the structural ceiling.

prompt: A 125 V, 20 A receptacle is installed in a non-dwelling indoor wet location subject to wash-down. Which personnel-protection rule applies?

options.text: AFCI only, because 210.12 is limited to dwelling units
No GFCI, because 20 A commercial receptacles are exempt
GFCI protection under 210.8(B) for other than dwelling units
GFCI only if that receptacle is also located outdoors

explanation: 210.8(B) requires GFCI protection for 150 V-to-ground receptacles 50 A or less in listed other-than-dwelling locations, including indoor wet locations. AFCI in 210.12 is a dwelling arc-fire rule and does not replace GFCI shock protection in a commercial wash-down area.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies dwelling AFCI (210.12) to a commercial wet location. AFCI addresses arcing fire risk, not the 210.8(B) GFCI requirement.
distractorExplanations.b: Invented a 20 A commercial exemption. 210.8(B) covers 125 V 15 A and 20 A (and larger ratings up to 50 A in current cycles) in the listed locations.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats outdoors as the only 210.8(B) trigger. Indoor wet locations, garages, sinks, and rooftops are separate listed GFCI locations.

prompt: A 15 A, 120 V branch circuit will supply dwelling-unit bedroom receptacles and lighting. Besides the OCPD, which additional protection does 210.12 require?

options.text: GFCI, because bedrooms are listed in 210.8(A)
A Type 1 or 2 SPD at the service in place of AFCI
No AFCI if the circuit is NM-B in wood framing
Combination-type AFCI protecting that bedroom circuit

explanation: 210.12 requires AFCI protection of listed dwelling branch circuits, including bedrooms, to reduce fire risk from arcing faults. Combination-type AFCIs are the usual means. GFCI (210.8) is a different device for shock in wet/damp locations; an SPD (Article 242) does not satisfy 210.12.

distractorExplanations.a: Puts bedrooms on the 210.8 GFCI list. Bedrooms are an AFCI location in 210.12; GFCI is for bathrooms, garages, outdoors, and similar 210.8 sites.
distractorExplanations.b: Substitutes surge protection for AFCI. SPDs clamp transients; they do not detect series or parallel arcing the way an AFCI does.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats NM-B as an AFCI exception. Cable type does not remove 210.12 for dwelling bedroom circuits.

prompt: A feeder’s conductors have 230 A ampacity after corrections. The load is 220 A noncontinuous. What is the largest standard OCPD 240.4(B) permits?

options.text: 250 A, the next standard rating above 230 A
200 A, because the OCPD must stay below ampacity
300 A, because next-size-up always applies over 800 A
230 A, using a nonstandard breaker matching ampacity

explanation: 240.4(B) allows the next standard overcurrent-device rating above the conductor ampacity when that ampacity does not match a 240.6 size, the OCPD is 800 A or less, and 240.4(D) small-conductor limits do not apply. 230 A is not a standard size; the next is 250 A. 240.4(C) forbids this round-up above 800 A.

distractorExplanations.b: Rounds down to 200 A. 240.4(B) permits the next standard size up (250 A) for 800 A or less when ampacity is 230 A.
distractorExplanations.c: Applies next-size-up above 800 A. 240.4(C) requires conductor ampacity to be at least the OCPD rating in that range.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes a 230 A breaker exists. Standard ratings in 240.6 skip from 225 A to 250 A, which is why 240.4(B) exists.

prompt: A 120/240 V feeder in EMT has two ungrounded conductors and a grounded conductor serving linear loads (a 3-wire single-phase MWBC). How many current-carrying conductors count for 310.15(C)(1) adjustment?

options.text: Three, always counting the grounded conductor
Two; the linear 120/240 V neutral is not counted
One, counting only the larger ungrounded conductor
Four, adding the equipment grounding conductor

explanation: 310.15(E)(1) does not count a grounded conductor that carries only unbalanced current from linear loads on a 3-wire 120/240 V single-phase circuit. The two ungrounded conductors are the CCCs for adjustment. Count the neutral when it is a 4-wire 3-phase wye with nonlinear loads, or when it carries substantial harmonic current.

distractorExplanations.a: Always counts the grounded conductor. That is required for some wye harmonic feeders, not for this linear 120/240 V 3-wire MWBC.
distractorExplanations.c: Counts only one ungrounded conductor. Each ungrounded CCC occupies raceway heat; both hots count.
distractorExplanations.d: Counts the EGC. Equipment grounding conductors are not current-carrying for 310.15(C)(1) adjustment.

prompt: A panelboard is installed indoors. How far must dedicated electrical equipment space stay clear of unrelated piping and ductwork?

options.text: 3 ft above the enclosure, matching working-space depth
Foreign systems may occupy that zone if a drip pan is over the panel
To 6 ft above the equipment or the structural ceiling, whichever is lower
Commercial gear only; dwelling panelboards are exempt from 110.26(E)

explanation: 110.26(E) reserves the space equal to the equipment width and depth, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower, for the electrical installation. Foreign systems belong above that dedicated volume (with protection from leaks), not inside it. The rule applies to indoor panelboards, including dwellings.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 3 ft, a working-space depth figure. Dedicated equipment space is a 6 ft (or ceiling) envelope above the gear, not the 110.26(A) depth.
distractorExplanations.b: Puts drip-protected piping inside the dedicated zone. Protection is for foreign systems above the dedicated space, not through it.
distractorExplanations.d: Exempts dwellings. 110.26(E) covers indoor switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, and motor control centers in all occupancies.

prompt: A dwelling bathroom will have a 125 V receptacle beside the basin. What branch-circuit rule in 210.11(C)(3) must the journeyman follow?

options.text: A 15 A lighting circuit may also feed those bathroom receptacles
Bathroom receptacles may ride on a kitchen small-appliance circuit
One 20 A circuit may feed bathrooms plus the garage receptacles
A 20 A circuit must supply the bathroom receptacles and have no other outlets

explanation: 210.11(C)(3) requires at least one 20 A branch circuit for dwelling bathroom receptacle outlets, and that circuit shall have no other outlets. The exception allows other equipment only when the 20 A circuit supplies a single bathroom. Kitchen small-appliance circuits (210.11(C)(1)) and garage outlets are separate assignments.

distractorExplanations.a: Puts bathroom receptacles on a 15 A lighting circuit. 210.11(C)(3) requires a 20 A circuit for those receptacles.
distractorExplanations.b: Shares the 210.11(C)(1) kitchen small-appliance circuits with the bathroom. Those two 20 A circuits are for kitchen/dining receptacles, not bathrooms.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds garage outlets to the bathroom receptacle circuit. Garage receptacles are a 210.8 GFCI location and are not ‘other outlets’ allowed on the bathroom 20 A circuit.

prompt: A non-motor, noncontinuous 22 A load is proposed on 12 AWG copper THHN with 75°C terminations. May the circuit use a 25 A breaker?

options.text: No; 240.4(D) limits 12 AWG copper to 20 A protection
Yes; Table 310.16 lists 12 AWG at 25 A in the 75°C column
Yes, because the load is not continuous and 22 A is under 25 A
Yes, if the 90°C THHN column (30 A) is used for the breaker

explanation: 240.4(D) small-conductor rules cap 12 AWG copper at 20 A overcurrent protection unless a specific article (motors, tap conductors, and similar) provides otherwise. The 75°C ampacity of 25 A and the 90°C THHN value of 30 A do not override 240.4(D) for this ordinary branch circuit, so a 25 A breaker is not permitted.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats the 75°C ampacity column as the OCPD cap. 240.4(D) still limits 12 AWG copper to 20 A on ordinary branch circuits.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses load current versus breaker rating and skips 240.4(D). Noncontinuous status does not authorize 12 AWG on 25 A.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the 90°C column to pick the breaker. 110.14(C) and 240.4(D) still keep 12 AWG copper at 20 A for this circuit.

prompt: A 120 V branch circuit supplies a 16 A continuous sign 120 ft from the panel. Using copper (K = 12.9) and a 3% branch voltage-drop target (3.6 V), what is the smallest conductor that meets that target? CM = 2KIL / VD.

options.text: 12 AWG copper (6,530 cmil), sized only by ampacity
8 AWG copper (16,510 cmil), which exceeds 13,760 cmil needed
10 AWG copper (10,380 cmil), which is below 13,760 cmil needed
4 AWG copper (41,740 cmil), far above the calculated area

explanation: Required circular mils = 2 × 12.9 × 16 × 120 / 3.6 = 13,760 cmil. 10 AWG (10,380) is short; 8 AWG (16,510) is the smallest standard copper size over 13,760. NEC voltage-drop notes in 210.19/215.2 are informational (about 3% branch, 5% feeder plus branch), but journeyman work still sizes conductors so the load actually starts and does not overheat from excess current at low voltage.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at 12 AWG ampacity (20 A continuous-capable). 6,530 cmil is far below 13,760 cmil, so drop far exceeds 3%.
distractorExplanations.c: Picks 10 AWG because it carries 16 A × 1.25. 10,380 cmil is still below 13,760 cmil, so the 3% target is missed.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumps to 4 AWG. That size works but is larger than needed; 8 AWG already exceeds 13,760 cmil.

prompt: How many 12 AWG copper THHN conductors (0.0133 in² each) may be installed in ¾ in. EMT (40% fill area 0.213 in²) when more than two conductors occupy the raceway?

options.text: 9, using 60% fill as if the run were a nipple
22, using the full internal area of the EMT
16, 0.213 in² divided by 0.0133 in² at 40% fill
4, matching the 310.15(C)(1) four-CCC adjustment count

explanation: Chapter 9 Table 1 limits more than two conductors to 40% of the raceway cross section. ¾ in. EMT 40% area is 0.213 in²; 12 AWG THHN is 0.0133 in²; 0.213 / 0.0133 ≈ 16. Annex C matches that count. Nipple 60% fill and ampacity adjustment counts are different calculations.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses 60% fill, permitted for nipples 24 in. or less (Chapter 9 Note 4), not for a ordinary EMT run.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses 100% of the EMT area. Table 1 allows 100% only for a single conductor, not for a bundle of 12 AWG THHN.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses conduit fill with the four-CCC ampacity adjustment threshold. Fill is a geometric count; adjustment is a heat-count of current-carrying conductors.

prompt: A 3/4 in. EMT run between a 480 V motor disconnect and a starter uses listed couplings and connectors made up wrench-tight. When may this EMT serve as the equipment grounding conductor?

options.text: When the fittings are listed for grounding and the joints are made up tight
Only if a green insulated 12 AWG copper is pulled with the circuit conductors
Never, because a raceway may contain an EGC but cannot itself be the EGC
Only on 120 V circuits; 480 V feeders require a separate copper EGC

explanation: NEC 250.118 recognizes EMT as an equipment grounding conductor when the fittings are listed for grounding and the joints are made up tight. A separate wire EGC is not required solely because the circuit is 480 V. Listed wrench-tight EMT is a standard fault-return path on motor circuits.

distractorExplanations.b: A wire EGC may be added, but 250.118 does not require one inside listed, tight EMT just to qualify the raceway.
distractorExplanations.c: Several metal raceways, including EMT, RMC, and IMC, are permitted EGCs under 250.118 when fittings are listed.
distractorExplanations.d: Voltage class does not strip EMT of EGC status; the listing and tightness of the fittings control, not 120 V versus 480 V.

prompt: A 400 A service uses 600 kcmil copper ungrounded conductors. The grounding electrode system is two driven rods. What is the minimum copper grounding electrode conductor to those rods?

options.text: 1/0 AWG copper, matching Table 250.66 for 600 kcmil ungrounded conductors
6 AWG copper; rod, pipe, or plate taps need not exceed 6 AWG
4 AWG copper, matching the concrete-encased electrode (ufer) column
8 AWG copper, matching Table 250.122 for a 400 A feeder equipment ground

explanation: Table 250.66 would call for 1/0 copper to a water pipe or building steel on this service, but 250.66(A) caps the conductor to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode at 6 AWG copper. The rods cannot usefully take a larger GEC, so the Code does not require one.

distractorExplanations.a: 1/0 is the Table 250.66 size to metal water pipe or structural steel for 600 kcmil copper; 250.66(A) reduces the rod tap to 6 AWG.
distractorExplanations.c: 4 AWG copper is the usual minimum to a concrete-encased electrode under 250.66(B), not to driven rods.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 250.122 sizes equipment grounding conductors from the OCPD; GECs to electrodes use 250.66, with the 6 AWG rod cap.

prompt: Interior metal water piping used as a grounding electrode has an insulating meter coupling that can be removed for service. What bonding is required around that meter?

options.text: No jumper is needed if the meter body is listed as electrically continuous
Bond only the hot-water heater piping; cold water already serves as the electrode
Install a jumper only when the water utility requests it in writing
Install a bonding jumper around the meter so the electrode path stays continuous

explanation: 250.68 and 250.53(D) require a bonding jumper around likely-to-be-disconnected sections of metal water piping used as an electrode, including meters and insulating couplings. Removing the meter must not open the grounding electrode conductor path.

distractorExplanations.a: A listed meter body does not keep the path intact when the meter is pulled; the jumper bonds around the removable section.
distractorExplanations.b: The electrode connection is to the metal water piping system, not a hot-only loop; skipping the meter leaves a gap on the cold line.
distractorExplanations.c: The Code, not a utility letter, requires continuity of the electrode path around removable fittings.

prompt: A 60 A non-motor branch circuit is installed in Schedule 40 PVC with 6 AWG copper ungrounded conductors. What is the minimum copper equipment grounding conductor?

options.text: 8 AWG copper, using the 100 A column of Table 250.122
6 AWG copper, matching the ungrounded circuit conductors in the PVC
10 AWG copper, using the 60 A column of Table 250.122
12 AWG copper, using the 20 A column as if it were a receptacle circuit

explanation: Table 250.122 sizes the EGC from the rating of the overcurrent device, not from the ungrounded conductor size. For a 60 A OCPD the minimum copper EGC is 10 AWG. PVC is not an EGC, so that 10 AWG must be pulled and bonded at the metal enclosure.

distractorExplanations.a: 8 AWG copper is the 100 A row of Table 250.122, not the 60 A row.
distractorExplanations.b: Matching the 6 AWG hots oversizes the EGC; 250.122 does not require the EGC to equal the ungrounded conductors here.
distractorExplanations.d: 12 AWG is the 20 A row. A 60 A circuit is not sized as a 15/20 A receptacle branch.

prompt: A 20 A, 120 V circuit is pulled in Schedule 40 PVC from a panelboard to a metal disconnect on a rooftop unit. How is equipment grounding completed at the disconnect?

options.text: Pull a copper EGC in the PVC and terminate it to the metal enclosure
Rely on the PVC itself, because nonmetallic conduit is listed as an EGC
Use metal locknuts on the PVC hubs; the hubs bond the enclosure without a wire
Land the grounded (neutral) conductor on the disconnect’s grounding bar

explanation: PVC is not an equipment grounding conductor (250.118). A copper EGC sized from Table 250.122 must be pulled in the raceway and bonded to the metal disconnect so fault current has a path back to the source. Hub locknuts on PVC do not create that path.

distractorExplanations.b: Article 352 PVC is a nonmetallic raceway; it is not listed as an EGC the way EMT, IMC, or RMC can be.
distractorExplanations.c: PVC hubs and locknuts secure the raceway; they do not substitute for an EGC terminated to the enclosure.
distractorExplanations.d: The grounded conductor is not used as an EGC on the load side of the service; that would create objectionable current on the raceway and enclosure.

prompt: A 2 in. RMC containing 480Y/277 V feeders enters a metal enclosure through a concentric knockout that is not listed for bonding. What is required at that entry?

options.text: Standard locknuts on both sides of the box, because RMC is a ferrous raceway
A listed bonding bushing or locknut that bonds around the knockout
No extra bonding if the conduit is wrench-tight against the outer knockout ring
Change the RMC to EMT so concentric knockouts are treated as automatically bonded

explanation: On circuits over 250 V to ground, 250.97 requires bonding around concentric or eccentric knockouts unless the box or knockout is listed to provide a reliable bond. A bonding bushing or equivalent listed fitting jumpers the raceway to the enclosure past the weakened rings.

distractorExplanations.a: Ordinary locknuts may be acceptable on a single knockout listed for grounding; they do not replace 250.97 bonding on unused concentric rings.
distractorExplanations.c: Tightness on the outer ring still leaves painted, stacked KO rings in the fault path; that is the condition 250.97 is written to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: EMT has the same 250.97 duty at concentric KOs on >250 V circuits; changing raceway type does not skip the bonding fitting.

prompt: Listed flexible metal conduit is used as the wiring method to a 120 V, 20 A disposal. When may the FMC itself serve as the equipment grounding conductor?

options.text: For any length, provided the connectors are listed for grounding
On circuits up to 60 A if the FMC is 3/4 in. trade size or larger
In a wet location if the FMC has a sunlight-resistant outer jacket
Listed fittings, 20 A OCPD or less, and not more than 6 ft of FMC

explanation: 250.118(5) and 348.60 allow FMC to serve as the EGC only with listed grounding fittings, a circuit OCPD not over 20 A, and a total length not over 6 ft. Longer or larger-ampacity runs need a wire EGC inside the FMC.

distractorExplanations.a: Length is capped at 6 ft when FMC is used as the EGC; listed fittings alone do not lift that limit.
distractorExplanations.b: The OCPD cap is 20 A, not 60 A; trade size does not buy a higher EGC rating for FMC.
distractorExplanations.c: FMC is not a wet-location wiring method by default, and a jacket does not create EGC permission beyond 250.118(5).

prompt: An exposed 3/4 in. EMT homerun crosses a dry storage room and lands in a metal panel. What are the support and fastening intervals for that EMT?

options.text: Within 12 in. of each box and at 4.5 ft intervals, matching NM cable 334.30
Within 18 in. of each box and at 8 ft intervals, matching IMC in some tables
Fastened within 3 ft of each box or fitting and supported every 10 ft
Only at boxes; intermediate straps are not required on a straight, short run

explanation: 358.30 requires EMT to be securely fastened within 3 ft of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, or fitting and supported at intervals not exceeding 10 ft. NM’s 12 in. / 4.5 ft rule is Article 334, not EMT.

distractorExplanations.a: 12 in. and 4.5 ft are the NM-B support figures in 334.30, not the EMT fastening rule.
distractorExplanations.b: IMC (342.30) also uses 3 ft and 10 ft in the general case; 18 in. / 8 ft is not the EMT interval.
distractorExplanations.d: Even a straight homerun needs intermediate support at 10 ft and fastening within 3 ft of each termination.

prompt: Nine 12 AWG THHN conductors plus a 12 AWG EGC will be pulled in 1/2 in. EMT. What determines whether that count is permitted?

options.text: Chapter 9 Table 1 at 40% fill, using Tables 4 and 5 conductor areas
Table 310.16 ampacity only, because raceway fill is treated as a heating calculation
314.16 box-fill volumes applied to the EMT trade size as if it were a device box
Chapter 9 Table 8 bare-conductor areas, with no percentage fill limit applied

explanation: Raceway conductor fill uses Chapter 9 Table 1 (40% when more than two conductors) against the internal area in Table 4 and the insulated conductor areas in Table 5 (or Annex C). Ampacity tables and box-fill volumes do not set how many THHN wires fit in the EMT.

distractorExplanations.b: 310.16 sets ampacity after adjustment; it does not replace Chapter 9 percentage fill for the number of conductors.
distractorExplanations.c: 314.16 sizes boxes by cubic inches for 6 AWG and smaller; it is not the raceway fill calculation.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 8 is compact-strand and bare properties; insulated fill uses Table 5 against the Table 1 percentage.

prompt: A metal service raceway containing the ungrounded and grounded service conductors enters a metal service disconnect. How must that raceway be bonded to the enclosure?

options.text: By ordinary EMT set-screw connectors, the same method used on a branch-circuit homerun
A bonding jumper or 250.92(B) locknut, bushing, or threaded hub
Only if the inspector labels the enclosure as a separately derived system
By landing the grounded conductor on a bonding lug at every coupling along the riser

explanation: Metal raceways enclosing service conductors must be bonded under 250.92 using the methods in 250.92(B): threaded bosses, bonding locknuts or bushings, or bonding jumpers. Standard set-screw fittings that are acceptable on a branch EMT homerun are not the listed service-bonding methods.

distractorExplanations.a: Branch-circuit EMT set-screws may qualify the raceway as an EGC, but service raceways need the bonding methods of 250.92(B).
distractorExplanations.c: Service equipment bonding is required whether or not a separately derived system is present; SDS bonding is 250.30, not a substitute.
distractorExplanations.d: Couplings along the riser are made up as a raceway; they are not each a service-neutral termination point.

prompt: A metal 4 in. square box is supplied by PVC containing a 20 A circuit and a spliced copper EGC. What must be done with the metal box?

options.text: Leave the box unbonded; PVC is intended to isolate metal boxes from the grounding system
Bond the box only if a receptacle yoke will be installed on the cover
Connect the grounded (neutral) splice to a grounding clip on the box
Terminate the EGC to the box with a listed grounding screw, clip, or bushing

explanation: 250.148 and 314.40 require metal boxes to be connected to the equipment grounding conductor when an EGC is present. With PVC, that connection is a listed screw, clip, or grounding bushing—not the raceway. Device yokes are extra; the box itself must still be bonded.

distractorExplanations.a: PVC isolates the raceway, which is why the box needs a wire EGC connection; isolation is not permission to leave the box floating.
distractorExplanations.b: A receptacle yoke can bond a box when the yoke is listed for that, but 250.148 still requires the EGC to be connected at splices in the box.
distractorExplanations.c: The grounded conductor is not an EGC on the load side of the service; neutrals stay isolated from the box except at the service or SDS bond.

prompt: A 100 A feeder is run in 1 in. RMC with threaded couplings made up wrench-tight between two metal enclosures. Is a separate wire EGC required in the conduit?

options.text: No; listed threaded RMC made up tight qualifies as an EGC under 250.118
Yes; rigid metal conduit never qualifies, so a copper EGC must be pulled
Yes, but only if the conduit run exceeds 25 ft between enclosures
No, but only when the feeder overcurrent device is 20 A or less

explanation: 250.118 lists rigid metal conduit as an equipment grounding conductor when the fittings are listed and the threaded joints are made up tight. Unlike FMC, RMC has no 6 ft or 20 A cap for this use. A wire EGC may still be pulled for redundancy, but it is not required by 250.118.

distractorExplanations.b: RMC is one of the raceways expressly recognized as an EGC; “never qualifies” confuses RMC with PVC or non-listed flexible conduit.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no 25 ft length limit on RMC used as an EGC; that kind of cap belongs to FMC/LFMC conditions, not threaded rigid.
distractorExplanations.d: The 20 A / 6 ft limits apply to flexible metal conduit as an EGC, not to RMC.

prompt: Exposed EMT will be installed under a commercial parking-deck soffit that is a wet location. Which installation is permitted?

options.text: Indoor set-screw EMT and fittings, because the soffit keeps rain off the raceway
EMT with wet-location fittings and corrosion protection as required
EMT only if it is used as a sleeve for NM-B rather than for individual conductors
No EMT; wet locations require RMC or IMC and prohibit electrical metallic tubing

explanation: 358.10 permits EMT in wet locations when the raceway, supports, and fittings are identified for wet use and corrosion protection is provided as needed. A parking-deck soffit is still wet; indoor set-screw fittings are not the wet-location listing.

distractorExplanations.a: A soffit does not reclassify the space as dry, and indoor set-screw fittings are not identified for wet locations.
distractorExplanations.c: NM-B is not a wet-location cable; sleeving it in EMT under a parking deck does not make the method legal.
distractorExplanations.d: RMC and IMC are common in wet work, but 358.10 still allows EMT with wet-location fittings; it is not prohibited outright.

prompt: A PVC feeder from a 200 A service disconnect supplies a remote building subpanel. Where is the grounded conductor bonded to the metal enclosure?

options.text: At both the service and the subpanel so each enclosure has a main bonding jumper
Only at the subpanel; the service uses an equipment bonding jumper instead of an MBJ
At neither location if a ground rod is driven at the remote building
At the service only; the subpanel isolates neutrals from EGCs and the enclosure

explanation: 250.24 bonds the grounded conductor to the service enclosure with the main bonding jumper. On the load side, 250.24(A)(5) and 408.40 keep the grounded conductor isolated from EGCs and metal enclosures. The remote subpanel gets an EGC (or equivalent) with the feeder; a rod there is a grounding electrode, not a second neutral-enclosure bond.

distractorExplanations.a: A second MBJ at the subpanel parallels the neutral and EGC and puts objectionable current on enclosures and raceways.
distractorExplanations.b: The MBJ belongs at the service, not at a downstream subpanel; swapping them reverses 250.24.
distractorExplanations.c: A ground rod at a separate building does not replace feeder EGCs or authorize bonding the neutral to the subpanel enclosure on a four-wire feeder.

prompt: A pull box has one 2 in. raceway entering a wall and another 2 in. raceway leaving the adjacent wall (angle pull). What is the minimum distance between those raceway centerlines?

options.text: 8 times the 2 in. trade size, or 16 in., as used for a straight pull
4 times the trade size, because angle pulls are allowed to be shorter than straight pulls
6 times the 2 in. trade size, or 12 in., per 314.28(A)(2) for angle pulls
Equal to the 2 in. trade size; conductor bending radius is not a box-sizing factor

explanation: 314.28(A)(2) sizes angle, U, and similar pulls at six times the largest raceway trade size between entries in the same wall—here 6 × 2 in. = 12 in. Straight pulls through opposite walls use eight times (314.28(A)(1)). Mixing the multipliers is a common journeyman error.

distractorExplanations.a: 8× is the straight-pull multiplier in 314.28(A)(1), not the angle-pull distance between adjacent walls.
distractorExplanations.b: Angle pulls are 6×, not 4×; 4× is not a 314.28 dimension for these entries.
distractorExplanations.d: Pull-box sizing exists specifically to protect conductor bending; trade size alone is not the dimension.

prompt: A crew is placing the service disconnect for a new dwelling whose service conductors enter at an exterior wall. Where must that disconnecting means be installed?

options.text: Anywhere inside the building if those service conductors are in rigid metal conduit
In the bathroom if that room is the nearest point of entrance of the conductors
Readily accessible, nearest the conductor entrance, and not in a bathroom
Only behind a utility lock so the occupant cannot operate the handle

explanation: 230.70 requires a readily accessible service disconnect at the nearest point of entrance of the service conductors into the building. 230.70(A)(2) prohibits that disconnect in bathrooms. Conduit does not let you bury it deeper in the building, and occupant access is required.

distractorExplanations.a: Raceway type does not move the disconnect; 230.70(A)(1) still ties it to the nearest point of entrance.
distractorExplanations.b: Bathrooms are prohibited locations for the service disconnecting means even if they are closest to the entrance.
distractorExplanations.d: The occupant must be able to operate the service disconnect; a utility meter seal is a separate issue.

prompt: You are pulling 120/240-V service-entrance conductors for a one-family dwelling. What determines the minimum ampacity of those conductors?

options.text: The main breaker handle rating alone, with no Article 220 load calculation
Table 250.66, working backward from the grounding electrode conductor size
Article 430 motor tables using only the largest motor full-load current
The Article 220 calculated load, with ampacity meeting 230.42

explanation: Service-entrance conductors are sized from the Article 220 calculated load. 230.42 requires their ampacity to be at least that load (with the usual 125% continuous-load treatment). The main breaker, Table 250.66, and motor FLC tables do not reverse-size the service conductors.

distractorExplanations.a: A large main does not replace the load calculation; 230.42 sizes conductors from calculated load, not from the handle alone.
distractorExplanations.b: Table 250.66 sizes the grounding electrode conductor from the service conductors, not the other way around.
distractorExplanations.c: Article 430 sizes motor circuits. A dwelling service is an Article 220 building load, not a single-motor feeder.

prompt: A dwelling service has a metal water pipe, a concrete-encased electrode in the footing, and a driven rod available on site. Which electrodes belong in the grounding electrode system?

options.text: The water pipe, concrete-encased electrode, and rod, as each is present
The underground gas pipe at the meter, used as the sole grounding electrode
The single rod only, with no 25-ohm test and no supplemental electrode
Interior water piping 20 ft from where the pipe enters the building

explanation: 250.50 requires all electrodes present at the building to be bonded into one grounding electrode system. Metal underground water pipe, concrete-encased electrodes, and rods/plates in 250.52(A) are permitted electrodes. Gas piping is not an electrode, a lone untested rod needs a supplement, and interior water pipe beyond the first 5 ft is not the electrode conductor path.

distractorExplanations.b: 250.52(B) prohibits metal underground gas piping from being used as a grounding electrode.
distractorExplanations.c: 250.53(A)(2) requires a supplemental electrode unless that single rod is shown to be 25 ohms or less.
distractorExplanations.d: 250.68(C) limits interior metal water piping used as a grounding conductor to the first 5 ft from entrance.

prompt: Open overhead service conductors run along a dwelling wall that has operable windows and a porch. What clearance from those openings is required?

options.text: Three feet from doors and porches only; operable windows are exempt
Three feet from operable windows, doors, porches, and similar openings
Whatever the utility specifies, because NEC clearances stop at the meter
The roof vertical clearances in 230.24(A), which also cover wall openings

explanation: 230.9(A) requires 3 ft of clearance from windows designed to be opened, doors, porches, balconies, and similar openings, except above the top of a window. Premises overhead service conductors are still under Article 230. Roof clearances in 230.24(A) are a different rule and do not replace opening clearances.

distractorExplanations.a: Operable windows are in the 230.9(A) list with doors, porches, and balconies; they are not exempt.
distractorExplanations.c: On the premises side of the service point, Article 230 clearance rules still apply to overhead service conductors.
distractorExplanations.d: 230.24(A) is roof clearance. Clearance from building openings is 230.9, not the roof table.

prompt: A dwelling has a meter socket on the outside wall and a separate main breaker enclosure a few feet away. What is that meter socket?

options.text: The 230.70 service disconnect, because pulling the meter isolates the premises
Utility-owned equipment in every jurisdiction, so the customer never furnishes it
A metering enclosure at the utility interface, not the disconnect unless combined
The point where service-entrance conductors end and feeder conductors begin

explanation: A stand-alone meter socket is a metering enclosure at the utility/customer interface. It does not open the circuit the way a 230.70 disconnect does unless the equipment is a listed combination meter-main. Service conductors generally end at the service disconnect, which is where feeders begin. Socket ownership varies by utility.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling a meter is not the required disconnecting means; 230.70 still needs a listed service disconnect.
distractorExplanations.b: Many utilities require the customer to furnish and install the socket to their spec; ownership is not universal.
distractorExplanations.d: Feeders begin at the load side of the service equipment, not at the meter jaws of a separate socket.

prompt: One dwelling is fed from a pole with an overhead span to the weatherhead. The house next door is fed from a buried utility run in the street to the meter. How are those two supplies named?

options.text: The buried run is a service drop; the overhead span is a service lateral
The buried run is a meter-to-panel service-entrance conductor; the overhead span is only a drop to the weatherhead
Both utility runs are customer-owned service-entrance conductors under Article 230
The buried utility run is a service lateral; the overhead span is a service drop

explanation: A service drop is the overhead utility conductors to the service point. A service lateral is the underground equivalent. Customer service-entrance conductors are a separate Article 230 category, typically from the service point to the service disconnect, not the utility drop or lateral itself.

distractorExplanations.a: The names are reversed: drop is overhead, lateral is underground.
distractorExplanations.b: Meter-to-panel conductors are service-entrance conductors. The buried utility run to the meter is the lateral.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops and laterals are the utility supply to the service point, not the customer’s service-entrance conductors.

prompt: A 400-A service uses two conductors in parallel per phase. What must be true of those paralleled conductors?

options.text: Same length, conductor material, size, and termination for each phase set
1/0 AWG or larger, with unequal lengths allowed if that eases the pull
Same size per phase, with mixed copper and aluminum allowed in one phase
Each phase in its own metal raceway and the grounded conductor in a fourth

explanation: Paralleled conductors (310.10) must be the same length, material, circular mil area, and insulation, and they must use the same terminating method, so they share current. 1/0 AWG is the usual minimum size, but length still must match. Mixing metals in a phase, or splitting phases into separate ferrous raceways, creates unequal impedance and inductive heating.

distractorExplanations.b: 1/0 AWG is the typical minimum, but paralleled conductors of a phase must still be the same length to share current.
distractorExplanations.c: Material must match within the paralleled set; copper and aluminum in one phase will not share current equally.
distractorExplanations.d: 300.20 requires all phase conductors and the grounded conductor of the circuit in each metal raceway.

prompt: An installer wants to land equipment on the line side of the service disconnect. Which connections does 230.82 actually permit there?

options.text: Ordinary branch circuits, if each circuit has its own overcurrent device
Listed supply-side items such as metering, certain surge devices, and permitted PV taps
Nothing except the meter enclosure; all other line-side gear is forbidden
Feeder panelboards rated at 125 percent of the service-conductor ampacity

explanation: 230.82 is a short list: cable limiters, meters and meter disconnects, instrument transformers, surge protective devices, supply-side PV connections, and similar listed items. General branch circuits and feeder panelboards connect on the load side of the service disconnect. The meter is permitted, but it is not the only permitted item.

distractorExplanations.a: General branch circuits are load-side. A local breaker does not authorize a 230.82 line-side tap.
distractorExplanations.c: 230.82 lists several permitted line-side items beyond the meter, including surge devices and certain PV connections.
distractorExplanations.d: Feeder panelboards are supplied from the load side of the service disconnect, not from 230.82.

prompt: A 120/240-V dwelling service supplies mixed 120-V lighting and 240-V equipment. What current does the grounded (neutral) service conductor carry?

options.text: Full ungrounded-conductor current even when 240-V line-to-line loads are balanced
Only the current of 240-V loads such as a range or water-heater element
Unbalanced 120-V load current, plus harmonic return from nonlinear loads
Negligible current, because the neutral is bonded to the grounding electrode

explanation: On a 120/240-V service the grounded conductor returns the unbalanced 120-V load. Line-to-line 240-V loads cancel on the neutral. Nonlinear loads can add triplen harmonic current. Bonding the neutral to the electrode at the service does not stop that load current from flowing on the grounded conductor back to the source.

distractorExplanations.a: Balanced line-to-line current cancels in the neutral; the neutral is not sized as a third ungrounded conductor for that reason.
distractorExplanations.b: Pure 240-V line-to-line loads draw no neutral current; 120-V unbalance is what the neutral carries.
distractorExplanations.d: The bonding jumper creates a fault path; it does not eliminate normal unbalanced load current on the neutral.

prompt: You are selecting the service disconnecting means for a new one-family dwelling. What is the NEC minimum rating?

options.text: 60 A, which 230.79 sets as the one-family dwelling service minimum
The arithmetic sum of every branch-circuit breaker handle in the panelboard
The kVA nameplate of the utility transformer that serves the lot
The Article 220 load, and not less than 100 A for a one-family dwelling

explanation: Service equipment must be at least the Article 220 calculated load. 230.79(C) also sets a 100 A floor for a one-family dwelling disconnect. 60 A is not that dwelling minimum. Breaker-handle totals ignore demand factors, and the utility transformer rating is not the NEC service size.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) is 100 A for a one-family dwelling. 60 A is a smaller-occupancy minimum, not this dwelling floor.
distractorExplanations.b: Article 220 applies demand factors. Adding breaker handles oversizes the service and is not the Code method.
distractorExplanations.c: The serving transformer kVA does not set the premises service rating under 230.79 or Article 220.

prompt: The serving utility marks the service point on a dwelling job. What does that demarcation determine for the electrician?

options.text: The enclosure in which the main bonding jumper must be installed
Where utility conductors and rules end and NEC premises wiring begins
The exact wall on which 230.70 requires the service disconnect to be mounted
The line beyond which the NEC no longer applies and only NFPA 70E remains

explanation: The service point is the boundary between the serving utility and the premises wiring. Utility rules govern on the supply side; the NEC governs the customer’s service-entrance conductors and equipment beyond that point. The main bonding jumper and the 230.70 disconnect location are equipment rules, not the ownership line. NFPA 70E is work-practice, not the service-point definition.

distractorExplanations.a: The main bonding jumper is installed at the service disconnect/service equipment, not automatically at the utility service point.
distractorExplanations.c: 230.70 sets disconnect location by nearest point of entrance of the service conductors, not by the painted service-point mark.
distractorExplanations.d: The NEC still applies to premises wiring past the service point. 70E covers electrical safety in the workplace, not ownership.

prompt: A feeder leaves the service equipment to a remote dwelling panelboard. How must the feeder overcurrent device relate to those feeder conductors?

options.text: It may exceed conductor ampacity freely if the feeder is shorter than 50 ft
It must protect the feeder conductors, generally not exceeding their ampacity
It can be omitted because the service main already protects every downstream feeder
It is taken from Table 250.66 using the feeder equipment grounding conductor

explanation: Feeders are protected under 240.4 and Article 215: the overcurrent device generally must not exceed the conductor ampacity after any required adjustments, with only the listed next-size-up and tap exceptions. A short run is not a blanket waiver. The service main does not replace feeder protection, and Table 250.66 is not an OCPD table.

distractorExplanations.a: Length alone is not a license to oversize the breaker; 240.21 tap rules are specific and limited, not a 50-ft free pass.
distractorExplanations.c: The service OCPD protects the service conductors. Each feeder still needs its own protection unless a true tap rule applies.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 250.66 sizes grounding electrode conductors, not feeder breakers.

prompt: A candidate says a dwelling service overcurrent device cannot exceed a “Class 160” 160-A maximum. What does the NEC actually set?

options.text: 60 A as both the minimum and the maximum for any dwelling service
160 A as the dwelling-service maximum in 230.79
No 160-A cap; 100–400 A services are common as the calculated load requires
200 A as the largest service permitted for a one-family dwelling

explanation: 230.79 sets minimum disconnect ratings (100 A for a one-family dwelling), not a 160 A ceiling. Dwelling services are routinely 100, 200, 320, or 400 A when Article 220 supports them. “Class 160” is not an NEC dwelling-service class. 60 A is not the one-family floor, and 200 A is not a Code maximum.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) is a 100 A one-family minimum, not a 60 A min-and-max for dwellings.
distractorExplanations.b: 230.79 is a minimum-rating rule. It does not create a 160 A dwelling maximum.
distractorExplanations.d: The NEC does not cap one-family services at 200 A; larger services are used when the calculated load requires them.

prompt: A one-family dwelling is being wired to a recent NEC cycle that includes 230.85. Where must the emergency disconnect be located?

options.text: Only if the service is larger than 400 A; smaller dwellings are exempt
Indoors, mounted immediately beside the interior panelboard
At multifamily buildings; one- and two-family dwellings are exempt
Outdoors, readily accessible, and identified as an emergency disconnect

explanation: 230.85 requires a readily accessible outdoor emergency disconnect for one- and two-family dwellings so first responders can de-energize the premises. It is not limited to services over 400 A, it is not an indoor-beside-the-panel rule, and the requirement targets one- and two-family dwellings rather than exempting them.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.85 applies to one- and two-family dwelling services without a 400 A threshold.
distractorExplanations.b: The emergency disconnect is an outdoor, readily accessible device, not an indoor handle next to the panel.
distractorExplanations.c: The rule is written for one- and two-family dwellings; it does not flip the scope to multifamily only.

prompt: An underground service raceway enters a dwelling below grade and turns up into the meter-main. What sealing requirement applies?

options.text: Seal the entry to limit moisture and gas, using a sealant identified for the insulation
Seal overhead masts only; underground service raceways are left open to drain
Use any expanding foam, because insulation compatibility is not a Code issue
Leave the raceway unsealed, because a seal would trap condensation in the pipe

explanation: 230.8 and 300.5(G) require sealing underground raceways where they enter buildings so moisture and gases do not migrate into equipment. The sealant must be identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation. Overhead-only sealing, random foam, and a ban on seals reverse those rules.

distractorExplanations.b: 300.5(G) is aimed at raceways entering from underground, where moisture and gas travel inside the pipe.
distractorExplanations.c: The sealant must be identified for the conductor insulation; unlisted foam can damage insulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealing is required to keep moist air and gases out of the equipment, not prohibited as a condensation trap.

prompt: A 480 V MCC bucket must be racked for troubleshooting and has no incident-energy label. Before energized work, an arc-flash risk assessment is required. What does that assessment primarily establish?

options.text: Available fault current used only to upsize the service overcurrent device
Rubber insulating glove class from the shock voltage of the bus
Which lockout steps may be skipped because live work is planned
Arc-rated PPE and the arc-flash boundary for the assigned task

explanation: NFPA 70E arc-flash risk assessment uses available fault current and clearing time to estimate incident energy. That result sets the arc-flash boundary and the arc-rated PPE (or PPE category) for justified energized work. It does not size service overcurrent devices, select glove class, or waive lockout.

distractorExplanations.a: Fault current comes from a short-circuit study (NEC 110.24) to rate equipment; arc-flash analysis uses it to find incident energy, not to resize the service main.
distractorExplanations.b: Glove class is a shock-risk decision from voltage and ASTM D120; arc-flash analysis sets arc-rated clothing and the arc boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: An assessment never authorizes skipping LOTO; it only specifies PPE and boundaries when energized work is justified.

prompt: A 50 hp 480 V pump will be uncoupled for a seal change. The local disconnect is opened. What must the crew still do before anyone puts a hand in the coupling?

options.text: Apply personal locks, release stored energy, and verify residual voltage is gone
Tag the disconnect without locking because the pump coupling is already off
Jog the starter once to prove the motor cannot start, then begin the seal work
Wait thirty seconds for the field to collapse, then start work without testing

explanation: OSHA 1910.147 and NFPA 70E require isolation, personal lockout, control of stored energy (rotation, springs, capacitors), and a proven absence of voltage before contact. Uncoupling the pump does not replace locks or a zero-energy test on a 480 V motor circuit.

distractorExplanations.b: A tag without a personal lock does not prevent someone from reclosing the disconnect; uncoupling is not a substitute for LOTO.
distractorExplanations.c: Jogging can start the machine unexpectedly and is not a verification method; isolation must be proven dead, not bumped.
distractorExplanations.d: Time delay does not prove de-energization; residual voltage and stored mechanical energy must be tested and released.

prompt: A 277 V lighting contactor must stay energized for in-service voltage checks. The journeyman needs hand tools at the terminals. How must those tools be rated?

options.text: To OSHA Class 00 glove voltage, because the tool rating follows glove class
To the printed arc-flash PPE category stamped on the insulated tool handle
To ASTM F1505/IEC 60900 insulation, typically 1000 V, jackets intact
By the UL file number on the jaw, treated as the insulation voltage rating

explanation: Insulated hand tools for live work are rated under ASTM F1505 / IEC 60900, commonly 1000 V, and the insulation must be intact. Glove classes, arc-flash PPE categories, and listing file numbers are different systems and do not set the tool voltage rating.

distractorExplanations.a: Class 00 (500 V ac) is an ASTM D120 rubber-glove class, not the rating system for insulated pliers or screwdrivers.
distractorExplanations.b: PPE categories describe arc-rated clothing; they are not a voltage rating printed as a tool insulation class.
distractorExplanations.d: A UL file number identifies a listed product; it is not the 1000 V insulation rating required for live-work tools.

prompt: A helper contacts a 277 V conductor and is unresponsive on the floor. The circuit is still energized. What is the first safe action?

options.text: De-energize from a safe place, call EMS, then start CPR if the scene is safe
Grab the victim’s clothing and pull them clear of the still-live conductor
Throw water on the panel so a ground-fault current will open the breaker
Wait for the victim to regain consciousness before calling EMS or a supervisor

explanation: Rescuers must not become a second victim. Open or trip the source from a safe place, summon EMS, then begin CPR or AED use only after the scene is de-energized or the victim is clear of the circuit. Direct contact with a live victim or wetting equipment is unsafe.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulling a person who is still on an energized conductor puts the rescuer in the current path.
distractorExplanations.c: Water on energized gear creates additional shock and does not reliably clear the fault.
distractorExplanations.d: Electrical shock can stop the heart; delayed EMS and CPR worsen outcomes even if the person looks merely stunned.

prompt: A VFD-fed 40 hp motor is locked out at the disconnect. The journeyman must land a new EGC at the drive terminals. Which remaining hazard must still be controlled?

options.text: Line-side residual only; load terminals are dead as soon as the disconnect opens
Dynamic braking that makes shaft coasting impossible after the stop command
No meter check at the VFD, because the locked disconnect is proof enough
Stored energy in the DC bus capacitors until discharged and verified dead

explanation: Opening a motor disconnect isolates the line but does not instantly drain a VFD DC bus. Capacitors can hold hazardous voltage for minutes. LOTO for electronic drives includes waiting the manufacturer’s discharge time, using bleed paths if provided, and proving absence of voltage at the DC bus and motor terminals.

distractorExplanations.a: Load-side and DC-bus terminals can remain live after the disconnect opens; residual energy is not limited to the line lugs.
distractorExplanations.b: Many VFDs coast on stop; braking is not guaranteed and does not remove electrical stored energy.
distractorExplanations.c: A locked disconnect is isolation, not verification; NFPA 70E still requires an absence-of-voltage test at the work point.

prompt: A 208Y/120 V panel is locked out. Before landing new branch conductors, the journeyman must prove the meter works. What is the live-dead-live sequence?

options.text: Watch the circuit go live, then dead after switching, then live again after restore
Prove two phases dead and treat the third as dead if those two readings match
Test the meter on a known live source, prove the circuit dead, then retest live
Check the calibration sticker on the meter and skip the known-live source checks

explanation: Live-dead-live proves the instrument, not the switching history. Test on a known energized source, measure every conductor on the locked-out circuit, then retest the meter on the known live source so a failed tester cannot be mistaken for a dead circuit.

distractorExplanations.a: The sequence checks the tester before and after, not whether the panel was recently energized or restored.
distractorExplanations.b: Each ungrounded conductor and the grounded conductor must be tested; two dead phases do not prove the third.
distractorExplanations.d: A current calibration sticker does not prove the meter works at this moment; known-live checks are still required.

prompt: A Class A GFCI on a 20 A construction receptacle trips when a helper uses a wet drill. What current condition caused that trip?

options.text: An arcing signature on the ungrounded conductor, which is AFCI protection
About 4–6 mA imbalance between the hot and the grounded conductor
More than 30 mA residual current, the typical equipment GFPE level
Fault current on the equipment grounding conductor that then trips the breaker

explanation: A Class A GFCI compares current leaving on the ungrounded conductor with current returning on the grounded conductor and trips at about 4–6 mA. That personnel threshold is far below 30 mA GFPE and is not the same function as an AFCI or a overcurrent device clearing via the EGC.

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting parallel or series arcing is an AFCI function; a GFCI does not look for arc signatures.
distractorExplanations.c: 30 mA is a common equipment ground-fault (GFPE) setting; it is too high for Class A personnel protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaker trip via the EGC is overcurrent/ground-fault clearing of large current, not a 5 mA differential trip.

prompt: Covers are off a 480 V motor-control bus. The restricted approach boundary is marked. Who may cross it to take a voltage reading?

options.text: A qualified person using shock PPE rated for the exposed voltage
An unqualified helper if a qualified person walks beside them
Anyone in arc-rated clothing, because clothing also covers shock risk
A qualified person without shock PPE if the meter reading takes under a minute

explanation: The restricted approach boundary is a shock boundary. NFPA 70E allows only a qualified person inside it, with insulating PPE and insulated tools as the voltage requires. Escort rules apply at the limited approach boundary, not the restricted boundary, and arc-rated clothing does not replace shock protection.

distractorExplanations.b: An escort may take an unqualified person to the limited approach boundary, not across the restricted shock boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc-rated clothing addresses incident energy; crossing the restricted boundary is a shock decision that needs insulated PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Task duration does not waive shock PPE inside the restricted approach boundary.

prompt: A 25 hp 480 V motor in a mechanical room is served from an MCC two rooms away. For ordinary servicing at the motor, what does NEC 430.102 require?

options.text: A remote emergency-stop pushbutton used in place of the motor disconnecting means
No local disconnect if the MCC bucket nameplate already lists this motor ID
No motor disconnect when the controller disconnect is located in another building
A lockable disconnect in sight of the motor unless a Code exception applies

explanation: NEC 430.102(B) requires a disconnecting means in sight from the motor location, and it must be lockable. Limited exceptions exist for some industrial installations with documented safety procedures. An E-stop, a nameplate, or a remote controller disconnect does not by itself meet the in-sight motor disconnect rule.

distractorExplanations.a: An E-stop may drop a starter coil; it is not the lockable disconnecting means required at the motor.
distractorExplanations.b: Identification of the MCC bucket helps lockout but does not place a disconnect in sight of the motor.
distractorExplanations.c: Distance to the controller makes an in-sight motor disconnect more necessary, not optional.

prompt: A journeyman must replace lamps from a ladder next to an exposed 277 V lighting busway. What ladder practice is required?

options.text: An aluminum ladder kept about 3 ft from the energized busway
A wood ladder painted so cracks in the side rails cannot collect moisture
Nonconductive side rails, or stay clear of the exposed energized parts
A metal ladder bonded to the enclosure before the worker climbs

explanation: OSHA and NFPA 70E expect nonconductive ladders near exposed live parts, or else maintained clearance so the ladder cannot contact them. Conductive rails put the worker in a fault path; paint on wood hides defects; bonding a metal ladder does not make contact safe.

distractorExplanations.a: Aluminum is conductive; OSHA overhead-line clearance for up to 50 kV is 10 ft, not a 3 ft busway exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Opaque coatings on wood ladders are prohibited because they hide cracks and other defects.
distractorExplanations.d: Bonding a metal ladder still leaves the climber in the path if the rail touches 277 V parts.

prompt: An unlabeled 480 V switchgear cubicle will have covers removed for an infrared scan. Why are untreated cotton work clothes not enough?

options.text: Incident energy at 480 V can exceed cotton and needs arc-rated PPE
480 V cannot sustain an arcing fault, so voltage-rated gloves are enough
Arc flash is a concern on 13.8 kV gear and is treated as negligible at 480 V
Infrared work is non-contact, so NFPA 70E clothing rules do not apply here

explanation: Low-voltage switchgear can produce high incident energy because fault current is large and clearing times can be long. Opening doors for IR work is energized work. Untreated cotton can ignite; arc-rated clothing, face protection, and a documented risk assessment are required even at 480 V.

distractorExplanations.b: 480 V systems readily sustain arcing faults; arc flash is a major hazard at this voltage.
distractorExplanations.c: Many severe arc-flash injuries occur on 480 V equipment; voltage class alone does not make it negligible.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing covers and working near exposed buses is energized work; non-contact IR does not waive 70E PPE.

prompt: A shock victim has a charred fingertip and a matching mark at the opposite boot. What do those paired marks indicate?

options.text: Surface-only burns, so internal tissue along the current path is uninjured
Current traveled through the body and damaged tissue along that path
Arc-flash radiant burns, which usually lack paired electrical contact wounds
A clothing static discharge that can closely mimic true electrical contact burns

explanation: Entry and exit burns mark where current entered and left the body. Damage along the path can include muscle, nerve, and heart injury that looks mild at the skin. That pattern is contact current, not purely radiant arc-flash burn or static.

distractorExplanations.a: Skin marks often hide deeper necrosis and cardiac effects; they are not proof the injury is superficial.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc-flash thermal burns can be extensive on exposed skin without classic entry/exit contact pairs.
distractorExplanations.d: Static discharge does not produce paired electrical contact burns of this kind.

prompt: Spare lumber and cardboard are stacked in front of a 480 V switchboard, leaving a walkway. What is wrong with that storage?

options.text: Storage is allowed if a 24 in. aisle remains in front of the switchboard
Ladders may occupy the dedicated space above the gear if the front stays clear
Required working space cannot be used for storage, and combustibles stay out
A locked electrical room waives the NEC 110.26 working-space clearance rules

explanation: NEC 110.26(B) forbids using required working space for storage. Combustibles next to switchgear add fire load and block emergency access. Dedicated equipment space above gear must also stay clear. Locking the room does not reduce the clearance dimensions.

distractorExplanations.a: A leftover walkway does not satisfy 110.26 depth and width; the working space itself cannot be storage.
distractorExplanations.b: 110.26(E) dedicated space above equipment is for raceways and ventilation, not ladder or material storage.
distractorExplanations.d: Access control does not waive working space; clearances apply whether or not the door is locked.

prompt: After LOTO on a 480 V motor disconnect, the journeyman must prove the load side is dead before lifting motor leads. What method is required?

options.text: Sweep a non-contact tester near each conductor and stop if the wand is silent
Open the breaker and rely on the panel schedule as the official dead check
Measure one phase-to-ground pair and treat the remaining phases as matching
Use a rated contact tester on each phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground pair

explanation: NFPA 70E requires an adequately rated contact instrument. Test phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground on every conductor, using live-dead-live to prove the meter. Non-contact wands, schedules, and a single pair can miss a still-live lead on a motor circuit.

distractorExplanations.a: Non-contact testers can miss shielded or low voltage and are not the accepted absence-of-voltage method.
distractorExplanations.b: Panel schedules are often wrong; documentation is not a voltage test.
distractorExplanations.c: One phase-to-ground reading can miss an open ground or a live remaining phase; all combinations are required.

prompt: A 480 V MCC bucket must be racked. Under NEC Article 100, who is a qualified person for that task?

options.text: Any state-licensed journeyman, even when untrained on this specific MCC
A person skilled on this equipment and trained to recognize and avoid its hazards
Anyone who finished OSHA 10 awareness training, without equipment-specific practice
An operator who has run the production line for years without electrical safety training

explanation: Article 100 defines a qualified person as one with skills and knowledge related to the construction and operation of the electrical equipment and who has received safety training to recognize and avoid the hazards involved. A license, OSHA 10, or operating experience without that training does not meet the definition.

distractorExplanations.a: A license is not the Article 100 test; qualification is equipment- and hazard-specific skills plus safety training.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA 10 is general awareness; racking an MCC requires training on that gear and its shock and arc-flash hazards.
distractorExplanations.d: Years of operation without electrical hazard training leave the person unqualified for exposed 480 V work.
